catalog_quote: In a recent study of Balti, (Caplow 2016) found fundamental frequency to be a strong correlate of contrastive stress, suggesting that the transphonologization of stress to tone is a pathway of tonogenesis. While Dzongkha does not have phonological stress, long and short rhymes are analogous to stressed and unstressed syllables (in contrast to Balti for which vowel duration is a weak correlate of stress). Perhaps what is seen here is a manifestation of the transphonologization of length to pitch: a contrast in the duration of the second syllable is manifest on the first syllable in elevated and suppressed pitch distributions, contributing to an emerging melody contrast on the first syllable. ... [p.141] Lexical words are those that take tone, can be uttered in isolation, and are not phonologically bound to any other word. ... Relational words (affixes and enclitics), on the other hand, a…
sweep_summary: Dzongkha (dzon1239, catalog no word stress on Watters 2018 Rice PhD, p.69 'Dzongkha does not have phonological stress'). this search of works with stress in the title has one item, Watters 1996 'A preliminary study of prosody in Dzongkha' (UT Arlington MA thesis, UMI/ProQuest 1383506, already in the per-language bibliography). No open copy exists: ProQuest preview only (saved), Harvard-restricted per the Harvard library catalogue, MPI-EVA CD-ROM per Glottolog, nothing on archive.org, HathiTrust, Google Books; UTA MavMatrix and sil.org record pages unreachable (not reachable by automated download). The author's own 2018 description (pp.6, 23) says the thesis is a segment-and-tone / phonation-pitch acoustic study whose content was folded into Watters 2002 (LTBA 25.1), which is held by the project and was re-read with the p.40 page scan verified: its only stress remarks are impressionistic scare-quoted 'stress' on long first syllables of disyllables in the Dzongkha/Lhomi syllable-tone type, illustrated with Lhomi data, and it concludes the syllable pitches are not phonologically contrastive. Net: the 1996 thesis is judged prosody-but-not-word-stress (unread, medium priority to acquire via ProQuest/ILL for completeness); nothing read this search of works with stress in the title supersedes Watters 2018; Watters 2002 p.40 refines the no-word-stress coding (length-linked prominence, no stress rule). searching was done by automated download/direct download on catalog APIs and known repositories only.

new_statements.quote: I now turn to a discussion of pitch when it is in the domain of the syllable, as in Dzongkha and Lhomi. The pitch pattern in disyllabic nouns for these two languages is considerably more complex than in monosyllabic words. I illustrate this discussion, again, with data from Lhomi. Vowel length is contrastive on the first syllable of disyllabic words, but not on the second syllable. When the first syllable is long it attracts stress, or perhaps it is because this syllable is stressed that it is lengthened. In any case, this syllable is "heavy" in comparison to the one which follows it. When the first syllable is short, the first and second syllables seem to be of equal "weight" in terms of quantity and "stress."
new_statements.citation: Watters, Stephen A. 2002. The sounds and tones of five Tibetan languages of the Himalayan region. Linguistics of the Tibeto-Burman Area 25.1: 1-65.
new_statements.locator: sec. 6.2 'Syllable tone (Dzongkha and Lhomi)', 6.2.1 'Potential patterns in nouns', printed p.40 = p.40; see also p.43 (first-syllable 'stress' as rising pitch in low register) and p.44 summary
new_statements.reading: For the syllable-tone type that Watters assigns to Dzongkha and Lhomi, he reports an impressionistic, scare-quoted 'stress' on a long first syllable of disyllables (long CVV.CV = heavy-light, short CV.CV = equal weight), with pitch (level/rising vs falling) derived from onset phonation and rhyme weight; the illustration is Lhomi data, not Dzongkha, and p.44 concludes the syllable pitches 'are not phonologically contrastive'. This refines the catalog's no word stress record (length-linked prominence, no fixed stress rule) but does not contradict it; the same author's 2018 grammar, the catalog's deciding source, states explicitly that Dzongkha has no phonological stress and treats long/short rhymes as merely analogous to stressed/unstressed syllables. Already logged as 'refines' in by the 2026-09-16 access pass.

tone_statements.citation: Lu, Qiyou (Ark). 2023. The Sound of Dzongkha: Recent Changes to its Tonal Paradigm. BA (senior) thesis, Department of Linguistics, Swarthmore College (Senior Theses, Projects, and Awards 896; advisor Amanda Payne).
tone_statements.quote: Two contrastive pitches are attested in this study, high and low, for all onset series. High vowels are attested following both aspirated and unaspirated onsets, while low vowels are only attested following unaspirated onsets. … Tonal contour is not attested to be contrastive in this study. … As a product of the underlying pitch of the vowel of a syllable and the prosodic position of the syllable, four syllable tones are attested: high falling, high rising, low falling, low rising.
tone_statements.locator: p.27, 4.4 Tone, opening lines; 'Tonal contour is not attested..' p.30; 'four syllable tones' p.31 above Table 19
tone_statements.summary: Two contrastive pitches, high and low (low never after aspirated onsets); tonal contour no longer contrastive, surface rise/fall set by phrase position; Praat F0 data from two speakers (Thimphu, Paro).

tone_statements.quote: While the Dzongkha high and low register and falling tone contour have been documented by Mazaudon and Michailovsky as well as van Driem, only the high and low registers were observed in the dialect of the consultant used for this study. … voiceless obstruent onsets occur only in the high tone (indicated here with a superscript H) and that voiced obstruents occur only in the low tone (superscript L). In addition, tone is contrastive after sonorant initials as they occur in both the high and low tone (see Appendix B). In other words, tone is lexical.
tone_statements.locator: pp. 68-69, sections 3.1 The Falling Tone Contour and 3.2 Obstruent Onset Voicing and Tone
tone_statements.summary: Two lexical register tones, high vs low, on the syllable; obstruent voicing and breathy initial vowels analysed as allophones of low tone; falling contour of earlier accounts not observed, set aside.

tone_statements.citation: Lee, Seunghun and Kawahara, Shigeto (2018). The Phonetic Structure of Dzongkha: A Preliminary Study. Journal of the Phonetic Society of Japan 22. pp. 13-20.
tone_statements.quote: From the previous studies (Tshering and van Driem 2015, Watters 2002), we know that Dzongkha has eight contrastive vowels, a two-way tonal contrast (H(igh) and L(ow)), and a four way laryngeal contrast [...] The tone is contrastive in vowel-initial syllables and syllables with sonorant onsets. However, there are tone-consonant restrictions in such a way that obstruents can be followed by only particular types of tones. Concretely, syllables with aspirated and voiceless onsets predictably bear H-tones, and "devoiced" and voiced onsets predictably bear L-tones (Tshering and van Driem 2015, pp. 39-40). [p. 13] ... It shows that H-toned and L-toned syllables are separated clearly at the onset of syllables, and the differences are neutralized toward the end for some vowels (see also Watters 2002 for a similar finding). [...] On average, at the onset of the syllables, H-toned and L-toned syllables differ by 30-40 Hz; the differences in F0 get smaller toward the end of the syllables, and are not observed in the fifth, final frame. What is emerging through our analysis is that tonal differences in Dzongkha most clearly manifest themselves at the onset of vowels. [p. 16]

tone.quote: From the previous studies (Tshering and van Driem 2015, Watters 2002), we know that Dzongkha has eight contrastive vowels, a two-way tonal contrast (H(igh) and L(ow)), and a four way laryngeal contrast [...] The tone is contrastive in vowel-initial syllables and syllables with sonorant onsets. However, there are tone-consonant restrictions in such a way that obstruents can be followed by only particular types of tones. Concretely, syllables with aspirated and voiceless onsets predictably bear H-tones, and "devoiced" and voiced onsets predictably bear L-tones (Tshering and van Driem 2015, pp. 39-40). [p. 13] ... It shows that H-toned and L-toned syllables are separated clearly at the onset of syllables, and the differences are neutralized toward the end for some vowels (see also Watters 2002 for a similar finding). [...] On average, at the onset of the syllables, H-toned and L-toned syllables differ by 30-40 Hz; the differences in F0 get smaller toward the end of the syllables, and are not observed in the fifth, final frame. What is emerging through our analysis is that tonal differences in Dzongkha most clearly manifest themselves at the onset of vowels. [p. 16]

sources.quote: While the Dzongkha high and low register and falling tone contour have been documented by Mazaudon and Michailovsky as well as van Driem, only the high and low registers were observed in the dialect of the consultant used for this study. … voiceless obstruent onsets occur only in the high tone (indicated here with a superscript H) and that voiced obstruents occur only in the low tone (superscript L). In addition, tone is contrastive after sonorant initials as they occur in both the high and low tone (see Appendix B). In other words, tone is lexical.

sources.quote: Dzongkha has a four-tone system, in which a high vs low register distinction (found in all syllable types) intersects with a level vs falling contour opposition (on some syllable types only--see below). We have numbered the tones in the order of their absolute pitch: 1 high-level, 2 high-falling, 3 low level, 4 low falling. On short open syllables, and on monosyllables in final -n, which have no distinctive contour, we have noted the registers as H and L. [...] (It is not clear that there is a tone contour opposition in the Paro dialect.)
sources.note: Consistent with the catalog's restricted-tone class and adds the system: 2 registers x 2 contours, contour contrastive only on long open and short closed rhymes (-V: -V~: -Vp -Vm; not on short open -V, not before -n; diphthongs and long closed rhymes are non-contrastively falling, Table 2 p. 118). Phonetics p. 119: tones 1 and 3 rise slightly and end in a glottal stop, tones 2 and 4 fall and end smoothly; before -p only an absolute-pitch difference, no contour. tone.quote: A preliminary analysis shows that “devoiced” consonants show lower F0 in the following vowel compared to voiceless consonants. [1] also notes that syllables with aspirated and “devoiced” onsets belong to H-tonal register, whereas those with voiceless and voiced onsets belong to L-tonal register. To expand on this observation, a 20 ms analysis window was created at the onset of the following vowel, and the average F0 within that analysis window was calculated for each type of consonants.
